questionText: What are generics and what constraints can you place on type parameters?
shortAnswer: Generics let you write type-safe code that works with any type (List<T>, Dictionary<TKey, TValue>), resolved at compile time with no boxing. Constraints (where T : class, struct, new(), notnull, interfaces, base classes) declare what capabilities the code requires from T.
detailedAnswer: Without generics you choose between object-based APIs (boxing, casts, runtime errors — ArrayList) or duplicating code per type. Generics give you both safety and performance: List<int> stores raw ints, and mistakes are compile errors. Constraints communicate requirements: where T : class (reference type, allows null), where T : struct (non-nullable value type), where T : notnull, where T : new() (parameterless ctor — must be last), where T : IDisposable or a base class/interface (member access), where T : U (type relationships), and where T : allows ref struct (C# 13, Span<T> in generics). Multiple constraints combine: where T : class, IDisposable, new(). Variance applies to interfaces/delegates: out T (covariant — IEnumerable<Cat> is IEnumerable<Animal>, output positions), in T (contravariant — IComparer<Animal> works as IComparer<Cat>, input positions). Generic methods infer type arguments (void Swap<T>(ref T a, ref T b) called as Swap(ref x, ref y)) and can be constrained independently of their class.
internalWorking: The JIT creates specialized native code per value-type argument (List<int> and List<long> get separate code) but shares one implementation across reference types (List<string>/List<object> share, with type checks where needed). Constraints are compile-time contracts plus runtime checks at the generic instantiation boundary — no virtual dispatch overhead for struct constraints in most cases (constrained. prefix).
realWorldUsage: Repository<T>, Result<T>, Option<T>/Maybe types, MediatR IRequest<TResponse>, System.Text.Json JsonSerializer<T>, and channels (Channel<T>) — generics are the backbone of reusable .NET libraries.
commonMistake: Using where T : class when you also need new() but forgetting the order (new() must be last), or constraining to struct then being surprised T? means Nullable<T>. Also: == on unconstrained T does not compile — use EqualityComparer<T>.Default.
technicalConversation: Ask why List<int> outperforms ArrayList by 2–5x in benchmarks — no boxing, no casts, dense storage, and devirtualized iteration all compound.
interviewFollowUp: How would you design a generic cache that works for both value and reference types without boxing?
keyTakeaway: Generics = compile-time safety + runtime performance. Constraints declare requirements; variance controls substitutability.

questionText: How does EqualityComparer<T>.Default avoid boxing, and when does it matter?
shortAnswer: EqualityComparer<T>.Default returns a specialized comparer: for types implementing IEquatable<T> it calls Equals directly with no boxing; otherwise it falls back to Object.Equals (which boxes value types). It matters in dictionaries, hash sets, and hot-path comparisons.
detailedAnswer: Comparing generics is tricky: you cannot use == on unconstrained T, and calling value.Equals(other) on a struct boxes both sides when Equals is the base Object.Equals(object). EqualityComparer<T>.Default solves this once, centrally: at first use it checks whether T implements IEquatable<T> — if yes, it returns a GenericEqualityComparer<T> that calls IEquatable<T>.Equals(T) with zero boxing; if no, an ObjectEqualityComparer<T> using Object.Equals. Dictionary<TKey, TValue> and HashSet<T> use it internally, which is why custom key types should implement IEquatable<T> (plus GetHashCode) — otherwise every lookup boxes. The same pattern exists for Comparer<T>.Default (IComparable<T>). For records, the compiler generates IEquatable<T> for you; for hand-written structs, implement IEquatable<T>, override Equals(object)/GetHashCode, and overload == / != — the full five-member pattern. In .NET 7+, generic math (INumber<T>) extends the idea to operators.
internalWorking: The Default property uses a static cache per T initialized in the static constructor: typeof(IEquatable<T>).IsAssignableFrom(typeof(T)) decides the comparer class. The JIT devirtualizes the interface call for sealed/value types, so the hot path is a direct call.
realWorldUsage: Dictionary keys (OrderId structs, composite keys), Distinct()/GroupBy() over structs in LINQ, and high-frequency event deduplication where boxing would dominate profiles.
commonMistake: Overriding Equals without GetHashCode (dictionary lookups silently fail), or mutable structs as keys (hash changes → entries lost). Also: record with a List<T> property — default equality compares the list reference.
technicalConversation: Ask how they would prove boxing in a lookup hotspot — allocation profiler showing boxed T in Dictionary probes is the tell.
interviewFollowUp: Why must GetHashCode never change while an object is a dictionary key?
keyTakeaway: Implement IEquatable<T> + GetHashCode on value types used as keys; EqualityComparer<T>.Default then compares with zero boxing.

questionText: What are delegates, Func, Action, and multicast delegates?
shortAnswer: A delegate is a type-safe function pointer: it declares a signature, and any matching method (or lambda) can be assigned. Func<T.., TResult> returns a value, Action<T..> returns void, Predicate<T> returns bool. A multicast delegate chains multiple handlers invoked in order.
detailedAnswer: Delegates decouple the caller from the callee: the caller knows only the signature. Declare delegate bool Filter(Item item); or use the built-in Func<Item, bool> / Action<string> / Predicate<Item> — modern code almost never declares custom delegates except for events (EventHandler<TEventArgs>) or meaningful domain signatures. Assignment accepts static methods, instance methods (capturing the target), lambdas, and method groups (list.ForEach(Console.WriteLine)). Combining with += builds a multicast invocation list; invoking calls each in subscription order, and -= removes the last matching entry. Exceptions: if one handler throws, later handlers are skipped and the exception propagates — for resilient notification, iterate GetInvocationList() with individual try/catch. Return values: only the last handler's return is visible, so multicast Funcs are rare. Variance: Func<string> is convertible to Func<object> (covariant return), Action<object> to Action<string> (contravariant parameter). Underneath, Delegate holds _target + _methodPtr; MulticastDelegate adds the invocation list — allocation per combine, so high-frequency += in loops is a (minor) cost.
internalWorking: A delegate instance stores the target object reference and a method pointer (or a closure object for lambdas). Invocation is an indirect call — JIT-optimized but not inlineable across the boundary. Combine creates a new delegate with a merged list (immutable operation, thread-safe publication).
realWorldUsage: LINQ (Where takes Func<T, bool>), callbacks (comparison, retry policies take Func<Task>), strategy injection without interfaces, and the plumbing beneath every C# event.
commonMistake: Forgetting delegates are immutable: handler += x inside a method without assigning back to a field does nothing (use the field: this.Changed += x). Also: invoking an event without a null check (use ?.Invoke) — classic NullReferenceException when no subscribers exist.
technicalConversation: Ask when they would choose an interface with one method over a delegate — testability/mocking and discoverability favor interfaces; brevity favors delegates.
interviewFollowUp: What happens to the return value and exceptions with five subscribers on one multicast delegate?
keyTakeaway: Delegates = typed method references; Func/Action cover nearly all cases; multicast invokes in order with last-return-wins and first-exception-stops.

questionText: How do events work in C#, and what is the standard event pattern?
shortAnswer: An event is a delegate with restricted access: external code can only += / -=, never invoke or clear it. The standard pattern is event EventHandler<TEventArgs> Name; raised via a protected virtual OnName method with ?.Invoke, using immutable EventArgs-derived data.
detailedAnswer: Events solve the notification problem with encapsulation. Declaring public event EventHandler<OrderShippedEventArgs> Shipped; generates add/remove accessors over a private delegate field — subscribers attach, but only the owning class can raise or reset it (unlike a public delegate field, which anyone could invoke or null out). The pattern: (1) EventArgs-derived payload (OrderShippedEventArgs : EventArgs with OrderId/ShippedAt), preferably immutable; (2) protected virtual void OnShipped(OrderShippedEventArgs e) => Shipped?.Invoke(this, e); — virtual so derived classes can override instead of subscribing to themselves; (3) generic EventHandler<T> (non-generic EventHandler for no data). Thread-safety: capture the delegate (var handler = Shipped; handler?.Invoke(...)) or rely on ?.Invoke, which the compiler lowers to a thread-safe temporary. Memory leaks: publishers outlive subscribers is the danger — a long-lived service exposing events keeps every subscriber alive; unsubscribe (-=) in Dispose, or use weak-event patterns. Async handlers: events are void-returning, so async void subscribers crash the process on exception — provide Task-returning notification methods (Func<T, Task>) instead of events for async flows.
internalWorking: The event compiles to add_Shipped/remove_Shipped methods plus a private backing delegate; += becomes Delegate.Combine loop (lock-free compare-and-swap in modern runtimes). ?.Invoke lowers to a temporary copy + null check, safe against unsubscribe races.
realWorldUsage: UI frameworks (button.Click), domain notifications in-process, file watchers, and any publisher/subscriber pair living in the same process (cross-process needs queues).
commonMistake: Leaking subscribers (never -= from a singleton's event), raising events with mutable EventArgs, and async void handlers whose exceptions tear down the process. Also: non-virtual OnX in a base class, forcing subclasses into awkward self-subscription.
technicalConversation: Ask how they would expose 'order shipped' to three microservices — events don't cross processes, so the answer should move to a message bus; in-process events and integration events are different tools.
interviewFollowUp: Why is async void acceptable for event handlers but dangerous everywhere else, and what is the safer alternative?
keyTakeaway: Events = encapsulated multicast with add/remove only. Immutable args, virtual OnX raisers, unsubscribe from long-lived publishers.

questionText: What can lambda expressions capture, and what are the costs of closures?
shortAnswer: Lambdas capture outer variables by reference into a compiler-generated closure object. Costs: one heap allocation per closure creation, extended lifetimes (captured variables live as long as the delegate), and accidental capture of loop/disposable state.
detailedAnswer: A lambda using no outer state compiles to a cached static method — zero allocation after warmup. The moment it reads an outer variable, the compiler generates a closure class holding those variables, and the variables' lifetimes extend to the delegate's lifetime (a captured DbContext in a cached Func leaks the whole context). Captured variables are shared by reference: two lambdas over the same variable observe each other's writes, and post-C# 5 each foreach iteration gets its own variable (pre-5 shared one — a famous historical bug), while for loops still share one variable across iterations unless copied inside. Costs to watch: allocation per closure in hot paths (prefer static lambdas: (a, b) => ... with the static modifier, which fails compilation if capture sneaks in), lifted structs, and capturing this (every instance-member access captures the whole object). Expression-bodied members and local functions follow the same rules; local functions avoid the delegate allocation when called directly but still close over state. In performance code, [MethodImpl] + static lambdas + passing state explicitly as parameters eliminates closure overhead.
internalWorking: The compiler emits a <>c__DisplayClass with public fields for captured variables; locals become field accesses. Non-capturing lambdas cache in a static <>c field. static lambdas are verified capture-free at compile time. Captured value types live on the heap from then on (no stack lifetime).
realWorldUsage: LINQ predicates closing over filter values, retry policies capturing attempt counts, event handlers capturing the sender context, and minimal-API handlers capturing services (watch lifetimes!).
commonMistake: Capturing the loop variable in for (fixed by copy), capturing a disposable/DbContext in a long-lived delegate, and capturing this unintentionally by calling an instance method inside a supposedly static lambda.
technicalConversation: Ask them to predict allocations of a LINQ chain in a loop — Where/Select allocate enumerator + closure each; a foreach with direct calls allocates nothing. Profilers confirm, but the mental model should come first.
interviewFollowUp: Why does marking a lambda static both document intent and improve performance?
keyTakeaway: Lambdas capture by reference into heap closures. Use static lambdas by default; copy loop variables; never capture short-lived resources in long-lived delegates.

questionText: How do switch expressions and property/list patterns simplify C# code?
shortAnswer: Switch expressions map inputs to values concisely; property patterns (Order { Total: > 100 }) destructure and test in one expression; list patterns ([first, .., last]) match collection shapes. Together they replace nested if/casts with exhaustive, compiler-checked logic.
detailedAnswer: Pattern matching tests shape, not just equality. Type patterns (if (response is OrderDto order)) combine check + declaration, replacing as + null-check. Switch expressions (status switch { 200 => "OK", 404 => "Missing", _ => throw ... }) are expressions returning values, with the compiler warning on non-exhaustive matches for enums. Property patterns nest conditions: order is { Total: > 1000, Customer.Country: "DE" }. Relational patterns (>, <, >=) and logical combinators (and, or, not) express ranges: age is < 13 or > 120. List patterns match spans/collections: [1, .., 9], [.., "end"], or [var first, ..] with captures — including Span<T> without allocation. not null replaces != null with clearer intent. The compiler analyzes exhaustiveness and unreachable arms; keep arms ordered specific→general since matching is top-down. Performance: patterns over spans avoid allocations; is-checks on sealed types devirtualize. Style rule: one level of nesting per pattern — deeper belongs in a named method or a separate arm.
internalWorking: The compiler lowers patterns to type tests, casts, and property loads — property patterns cache repeated sub-accesses in temporaries. Switch expressions over ints/enums can compile to jump tables; string switches use hash-based dispatch. List patterns over Span use length checks + element compares, no enumerator.
realWorldUsage: API result mapping (HTTP status → domain outcome), validation rule chains, message dispatch by shape, pricing/discount tiers, and parsing structured text via spans.
commonMistake: Unordered arms (general arm swallowing specific ones — compiler warns on unreachable, read warnings), matching mutable state that changes mid-check, and stuffing business logic into giant switches instead of polymorphism (strategy) when arms grow behavior.
technicalConversation: Ask when a switch should become polymorphism — one behavior per arm that changes independently is the strategy pattern's cue; pure mapping stays a switch.
interviewFollowUp: How does exhaustiveness checking differ between enum switches and type-hierarchy switches?
keyTakeaway: Patterns test shape concisely and exhaustively. Order arms specific→general; promote behavior-heavy arms to polymorphism.

questionText: What is reflection, what does it cost, and when is it justified?
shortAnswer: Reflection inspects and invokes types/members at runtime (typeof, GetProperties, MethodInfo.Invoke). Costs: slow invocation (~100x direct calls), no compile-time safety, trimming/AOT hazards. Justified for plugins, serializers, mappers, and tests — then cache handles and prefer source generators.
detailedAnswer: Reflection (System.Reflection) turns metadata into runtime objects: assembly.GetTypes(), type.GetProperty(name), method.Invoke(obj, args), Activator.CreateInstance(type). Legitimate uses: plugin discovery, serializers (System.Text.Json uses it unless source-gen), ORMs, test frameworks, and admin diagnostics. The costs are real: Invoke boxes arguments/returns, skips inlining, throws TargetInvocationException wrapping the real error, and breaks when obfuscators renames members or Native AOT trims unreferenced code (requires DynamicallyAccessedMembers annotations). Mitigations: cache PropertyInfo/MethodInfo (or compiled delegates via CreateDelegate / Expression.Compile — near-direct-call speed), validate names at startup (fail fast), and for new code prefer compile-time alternatives: source generators (JSON, regex, logging), static abstracts in interfaces (generic math), and merely switching on known types. Attributes ([Obsolete], [Required], custom [RetryPolicy]) are the metadata side — reflection reads them; keep attribute logic dumb and put behavior in the reader.
internalWorking: Metadata lives in assembly tables; MemberInfo objects are runtime wrappers. Invoke goes through the reflection stack (security checks, argument packing, exception wrapping) rather than a direct call instruction. CreateDelegate emits a direct stub. AOT trimming removes metadata for unreferenced members unless preserved — reflection then fails at runtime, a key reason libraries move to source generators.
realWorldUsage: Plugin/module scanners at startup, generic CSV/Excel exporters over DTO properties, test data builders, and migration/validation tools that walk entity metadata.
commonMistake: Reflecting per-record in a loop (move to cached delegates), GetProperty(name) with magic strings (rename breaks silently — use nameof where possible), and Invoke in request paths (orders of magnitude slower; profile first).
technicalConversation: Ask how they would design a plugin system for Native AOT — the answer must avoid runtime discovery (compile-time registration or source-generated manifests).
interviewFollowUp: What is the difference in failure mode between a missing member with reflection versus a source-generated accessor?
keyTakeaway: Reflection trades compile-time safety and speed for flexibility. Cache handles, fail fast at startup, prefer source generators for new code.

questionText: How does the .NET garbage collector work, and what are generations 0, 1, and 2?
shortAnswer: The GC reclaims unreachable objects. New objects go to Gen0 (collected often, cheap); survivors promote to Gen1 then Gen2 (collected rarely, expensive). The Large Object Heap holds big objects (85KB+). Write code that allocates little, keeps objects short-lived or permanently, and avoids mid-life crisis allocations.
detailedAnswer: The GC is generational and (by default) concurrent/workstation or server flavor. Allocation is a pointer bump in Gen0 — nearly free. When Gen0 fills, the GC marks reachable objects, compacts survivors into Gen1, and reclaims the rest — a Gen0 collection takes ~sub-millisecond. Objects surviving several collections promote to Gen1 (buffer) then Gen2 (long-lived: statics, caches, singletons). Full Gen2 collections are the expensive ones (all heaps, longer pauses — background GC mitigates). The LOH (≥85,000 bytes) is collected with Gen2 and historically not compacted (fragmentation risk; .NET 8+ compacts on demand). Finalizers delay collection by at least one extra cycle (object survives to the finalizer queue, then needs another pass) — implement IDisposable + SuppressFinalize instead; SafeHandle over raw IntPtr. Guidance: pool buffers (ArrayPool<T>), reuse collections (Clear over new), avoid mid-life allocations (objects surviving exactly one Gen1 = worst case), pin sparingly (pinning fragments), and measure with GC counters (% Time in GC > 5% is a smell) rather than calling GC.Collect (almost always wrong outside tests/benchmarks).
internalWorking: Each heap segment has an allocation pointer; allocation is Interlocked-free on the thread's allocation context. Mark phase walks roots (stacks, registers, statics, handles);compaction phase updates pointers (with pinning awareness). Server GC gives each core its own heaps + a dedicated GC thread (throughput); Workstation shares one heap with concurrent background Gen2 (latency). Card tables track old→young references so Gen0 need not scan all of Gen2.
realWorldUsage: High-throughput APIs (Kestrel parsers rent buffers), game loops and trading systems (zero-alloc discipline), and background ETL (batch + reuse to keep Gen0 small).
commonMistake: GC.Collect() in production code (disrupts self-tuning), event-handler leaks pinning whole graphs in Gen2, finalizers on managed-only wrappers, and string/closure allocations in per-request hot paths showing as Gen0 storms.
technicalConversation: Ask what they look at first in a memory-leak dump — Gen2 growth + reference chains (who roots the leak) via dotnet-gcdump, not task-manager megabytes.
interviewFollowUp: Why do mid-lived objects hurt more than either short-lived or permanent ones?
keyTakeaway: Gen0 is cheap, Gen2 is not. Allocate little, die young or live forever, pool buffers, never force collection.

questionText: What is the IDisposable pattern, and how do using, await using, and SafeHandle fit in?
shortAnswer: IDisposable releases unmanaged resources deterministically (files, sockets, handles). using calls Dispose at scope end (even on exception); await using handles async cleanup via IAsyncDisposable; SafeHandle wraps OS handles with finalizer safety. Implement Dispose + Dispose(bool) + SuppressFinalize when you own unmanaged memory directly (rare).
detailedAnswer: Finalizers run late and non-deterministically (extra GC cycles, no ordering, no async) — IDisposable exists so callers release now. The full pattern (for types directly holding unmanaged resources): public Dispose() → Dispose(true) + GC.SuppressFinalize(this); protected virtual Dispose(bool) frees managed (if disposing) + unmanaged; ~Finalizer() → Dispose(false) as backstop. In practice you rarely write it: wrap FileStream/SqlConnection/HttpResponseMessage in using (compiler emits try/finally + null-checked Dispose), use await using for IAsyncDisposable (async flush/close without blocking), and hold OS handles in SafeHandle derivatives (critical + reliable finalization, prevents handle recycling attacks). HttpClient is the famous exception: do NOT dispose per request (socket exhaustion) — use IHttpClientFactory singleton lifetimes. DI containers dispose scoped/transient IDisposables they create at scope end — another reason to prefer container-managed lifetimes. Ownership rule: whoever creates (or is explicitly given ownership of) the disposable disposes it; never dispose injected/shared instances.
internalWorking: using lowers to try/finally with Dispose in finally. await using awaits DisposeAsync in finally (state machine aware). SuppressFinalize clears the finalizer bit so the object dies in one collection instead of surviving to the finalizer queue. SafeHandle uses a critical finalizer + reference counting (DangerousAddRef) so the handle cannot be recycled mid-PInvoke.
realWorldUsage: File/network streams, DB connections (return to pool on Dispose — pooling makes open/close cheap), image buffers, timers, SemaphoreSlim (disposable!), and test fixtures (WebApplicationFactory).
commonMistake: Disposing shared HttpClient/DbContext-injected instances, forgetting await using for async flush (data loss on buffered writers), swallowing Dispose exceptions (they mask the original error — Dispose should rarely throw), and finalizers that touch managed objects (already collected — undefined behavior).
technicalConversation: Ask who owns a stream passed into their method — the answer (caller owns unless documented as transfer) reveals whether they have been bitten by double-dispose bugs.
interviewFollowUp: Why does returning a DB connection to the pool on Dispose make 'open late, close early' essentially free?
keyTakeaway: using/await using for deterministic cleanup; SafeHandle for raw OS resources; full pattern only when you own unmanaged memory. Never dispose shared instances.

questionText: What are Span<T> and Memory<T>, and when should you use them?
shortAnswer: Span<T> is a stack-only view over contiguous memory (arrays, stackalloc, native) with zero allocations and bounds checks; Memory<T> is its heap-storable, await-friendly sibling. Use them for zero-alloc parsing, slicing, and buffer pipelines.
detailedAnswer: Span<T> (ref struct — stack-only, cannot cross await or box) abstracts 'a pointer + length' over arrays, strings (ReadOnlySpan<char>), stackalloc buffers, and unmanaged memory with a single API: Slice, IndexOf, CopyTo, SequenceEqual. Parsing without substrings: ReadOnlySpan<char> input; while TryParse slices advance — zero heap traffic. stackalloc Span<byte> for small scratch buffers avoids ArrayPool ceremony. Memory<T> wraps the same for heap storage: hold it in fields, pass through async methods, then .Span to work — the bridge for pipelines (PipeReader returns ReadOnlySequence, Memory-based). Rules: never store Span in fields/lambdas/async (compiler enforces via ref struct); use ReadOnlySpan for inputs; prefer sequence-based APIs (IndexOf over manual loops — vectorized); for strings use AsSpan() + span overloads (StartsWith, Split via Span). Interop with older APIs via ToArray() only at boundaries. .NET's own stack (Kestrel, JsonSerializer) is span-based — following the same pattern aligns your code with the platform's fastest paths.
internalWorking: Span is (byref, length) — two machine words; the JIT bounds-checks then often eliminates checks in loops, and IndexOf/SequenceEqual map to SIMD (Vector128/256/512) instructions. stackalloc reserves space in the current frame (guard against huge sizes — stack overflow). ref struct enforcement is compile-time escape analysis (no runtime cost).
realWorldUsage: CSV/log parsers, protocol decoders (length-prefixed frames), Kestrel middleware buffer handling, high-frequency JSON field extraction, and image/audio sample loops.
commonMistake: ToArray()/ToString() mid-pipeline (reintroduces the allocations spans avoided), storing Span in a class field (compile error — use Memory<T>), stackalloc of kilobytes in recursive code (overflow), and slicing beyond intent (spans don't own — mutating a slice mutates the source, by design).
technicalConversation: Ask them to rewrite a Substring-based parser with spans and predict the allocation delta — then confirm with a one-line BenchmarkDotNet comparison.
interviewFollowUp: Why can Span<T> not be a field, and what breaks if you try to await while holding one?
keyTakeaway: Span = zero-alloc stack view, Memory = heap/async-capable view. Slice and parse without allocating; convert at boundaries only.
